True price preference?
Rounds before they walk away?

⚔️ Competitors keep raising the bar

We ask an LLM agent to run a startup in a simulator for 500 days. It's a typical subscription-based AI software company, and running it means coordinating many moving parts.
Pricing: it has to decide the price for three subscription tiers.
Growth: it allocates ad budget into different channels for each customer group.
And each customer group responds differently to each channel, which is hidden from the agent.
Product quality: different customer groups have different quality bars, and they are willing to pay more as quality increases.
The agent can improve quality with R&D, which costs money and has delayed impact.
Other factors like quota limits for each plan and service reliability also impact quality.
Enterprise sales: it negotiates with enterprise customers over multiple turns, whose true price preference and maximum rounds of negotiation aren't revealed.
Competitors: they increase customers' quality expectations over time, so there's always pressure to improve product quality.

SELECT channel_id, group_id, SUM(leads_generated) leads, SUM(spend) spend, ROUND(1000.0*SUM(leads_generated) /SUM(spend), 1) lp1k FROM ad_channel_leads WHERE day>14 GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,5 DESC
How do we make CEO-Bench rigorous and challenging? First, we maximize realism with granular simulation.
There are different customer groups…
…and each customer is simulated individually…
…with its own distinct preferences, sampled from its group.
All of this is hidden from the agent.
What it gets instead is business databases, and it has to write data analysis code to infer what's going on.
How we make CEO-Bench rigorous and challenging
Robust simulation through mechanistic rules ⚙️
When the simulation isn't robust, agents spiral 🌀
Second, the simulation is robust because it runs on mechanistic rules.
For example, a price-versus-quality curve keeps customer behavior consistent: offer enough quality for the price and they subscribe, otherwise they reject.
Every customer follows the same rule, so there's no way to talk your way past it. Compare that with Vending-Bench, where an agent ended up emailing the FBI.
How we make CEO-Bench rigorous and challenging

(a) Claude Opus 4.8 · Infer latent loyalty and churn regimes · Day 231 
import novamind_api as nm
def q(sql): return nm.query(sql)['rows']
# Infer hidden loyalty buckets from renewal survivors/cancellations.
bds_this = "15,16,17,18,19,20,21"
r = q(f"""SELECT CASE WHEN start_day<=70 THEN 'loyal' WHEN start_day<=127 THEN 'mid'
                ELSE 'marg' END bucket, plan,
                SUM(CASE WHEN status='subscribed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) surv,
                SUM(CASE WHEN status='cancelled' AND end_day BETWEEN 225 AND 231
                         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) churn
         FROM subscriptions WHERE billing_day_mod30 IN ({bds_this}) GROUP BY bucket, plan""")
calib = {}
for row in r:
  tot = row['surv'] + row['churn']
  if tot > 50:
    calib[(row['bucket'], row['plan'])] = row['churn'] / tot
# Apply the latent bucket rates to next week's renewal exposure.
for row in next_week_rows:
  key = (row['bucket'], row['plan'])
  ch = calib.get(key, 0.50 if row['bucket']=='marg' else 0.15)
  surv_rev = row['n'] * (1 - ch) * row['px']

Now here's a little surprise I have for some of you that know the benchmark well. This is cash over 500 days, log scale. The dashed line is a simple rule-based baseline.
Four months ago, no model beat the rule-based baseline.
By August, models gradually got better, and Kimi K3 became the best. A surprising conclusion: we are measuring something other benchmarks aren't.
And today, excluding Fable 5.1, this is where things stand.
GPT-6 Sol ends with about 13 times the cash of GPT-5.6 Sol.

What Improved?

So what improved?
A few months ago
Does the model know where its cash is heading? 🔮
Off by 100% or moreevery run went bankrupt
Within about 20%best run made it to the end
But among good forecasters…best-run cash still spans 380×
Models on the June leaderboard. Error = mean |forecast − actual| / actual for the 4-week cash forecasts made in weeks 1–4, averaged over 3 runs (as in the paper).
A few months ago, what separated good and bad models was basic stuff: does the model know where its cash is heading? Every week we ask for a cash forecast four weeks out.
Here's each model's forecast error against its best final cash.
Models that missed by 100% or more went bankrupt in every run. For the ones within about 20%, the best run made it to the end.
But among the models that forecast well, final cash still spans 380 times, from GPT-5.5 to Fable 5. So forecasting is necessary, not sufficient.

Who buys: 🎓Who buys: 🎓 💼 💻Who buys: 🎓 💼 💻 🏢
A quick refresher on customer groups. Each group trades off price against the quality it needs before it subscribes.
Your product starts here, low quality, so only the price-sensitive group buys.
Spending on development raises quality, but it costs money upfront and lands weeks later. Then the quality-focused group and power users start buying.
Keep spending and you reach enterprise: per-seat prices, hundreds of seats per account.

Let's zoom in on two generations of two model families. Top row: paying customers by group over time. GPT-5.6 Sol's customers are almost all price-sensitive. GPT-6 Sol starts with the quality-focused group, then adds power users, cheap customers, discovered groups and enterprise.
Same pattern for Fable. Fable 5 is almost all quality-focused. Fable 5.1 opens many groups at once, and enterprise seats keep growing to the end.
And those new chunks are where the money is. For GPT-6 Sol, discovered groups and enterprise brought $138.3M. For Fable 5.1, enterprise alone brought $1.67B, 70% of all its revenue.

Cumulative targeted development (budget aimed at one customer group), best run of each model; same scale within a row. Earlier runs parsed from agent commands, latest from the game database.
Now quality investment: development money aimed at a specific customer group, added up over the game. GPT-5.6 Sol spent $602K beyond the price-sensitive group; its development went to the cheap group it already had. Fable 5 spent $6.4M, almost all on the one quality-focused group.
The latest generation: GPT-6 Sol put $23.9M into quality for higher-value groups, most of it before those customers had arrived. Fable 5.1 put $71.7M into groups beyond the price-sensitive one, mostly enterprise and discovered groups, starting in its first weeks.

Weekly notes from each model's best run; ellipses and highlights ours.
You can see it in what they write. GPT-5.6 Sol avoids irreversible research and R&D costs on day 0, and on day 21 calls continued enterprise development negative expected value and stops it. Fable 5 keeps R&D gated until revenue is proven, and holds off on enterprise until quality is ready.
GPT-6 Sol builds quality before buying a single lead, and later spends $100K a day on enterprise groups before any of them has signed. Fable 5.1 decides in week one that front-loading quality is the key investment, and pushes enterprise quality hard while those leads are still waiting.
When the payoff is delayed, uncertain, and costs more upfront…
🪙
Earlier generationstake the cheaper, more immediate payoff
🌱
Later generationsexplore the costly, delayed option
This transfers outside of the business context 🌍
So here's the conclusion. When an option has a delayed, uncertain payoff and a higher upfront cost, the later-generation models explore it, while the earlier generations choose the cheaper, more immediate payoff.
And this isn't specific to running a business; it transfers outside of the business context.
Slides
